comment: Every difference between stack-up, stack-single and stack-k8s that somebody
has looked at and decided to keep. C5 fails on any divergence NOT recorded
here, and also on any entry here that is no longer a divergence.
'agreed' per family is the value the three are measured against. It is not
a majority vote and not an average: it is what the estate says the stack
is. Changing an 'agreed' value is a decision about the product, not a way
Provenance markers follow the estate convention: @claude is a reading of
the code and should be re-checked, @yurii is a decision, @measured names
the run that established it. Everything in this file was written by
reading the three repositories on 2026-08-06 and is therefore @claude.
The reasons are the honest state of the estate on that date, which in
several cases is 'this is a gap, not a decision'. That is deliberate: a
gap recorded as a gap is still better than a gap nobody wrote down, and
the entry is what makes it visible enough to close.

routines.what: Governance routines each deployment installs, by canonical kind.

routines:stack-up:disabled:mockryx-drill.why: Deliberate and documented in stack-up/routines.sh: mockryx-drill is opt-in behind --with-drill and never in DEFAULT_ROUTINES, because a fire drill spends real gateway budget against a live box. The other four are safe to run unattended.

routines:stack-k8s:disabled:mockryx-dril.why: Same decision as stack-up, expressed as `suspend: true` on the `drills` CronJob. The operator unsuspends it when they want a drill.

routines:stack-k8s:absent:focus-export.why:
CLOSED on 2026-08-28, and not by adding a CronJob, which was never possible. `tokenfuse-gateway focus-export --traces <dir>` reads the gateway's local Parquet directory off disk, and that directory is an emptyDir in 10-planes.yaml: mountable ONLY by containers inside its own pod, by Kubernetes' own design, so no Job could reach it whatever its affinity said.

The other way out was a PersistentVolumeClaim for the trace directory. That provisions a real disk billed from creation, which makes it a spending decision rather than a fix, so it was not taken.

It runs as a SIDECAR in the pod that already holds the volume, on an interval rather than a schedule, and prints rather than storing. That is what quality-drift does one file over: in this deployment a routine's artifact is its log. Recorded as a gap from 2026-08-06 and open for twenty-two days.

This entry stays as a DIVERGENCE rather than being deleted because it still is one: the other two deployments schedule this routine and this one does not. What changed is that it is now a decision with a reason instead of a hole.

routines:stack-single:absent:focus-expor.why: CLOSED on 2026-08-28. This deployment installed NO scheduler of any kind and now runs four routines behind `--profile routines`, as LOOPS rather than timers, because compose has no cron. That is the same shape the `record` profile already used. focus-export, as `routine-focus-export`. This deployment's `traces` is a NAMED volume rather than the emptyDir stack-k8s has, so a separate service can read it, which is why the same routine needed a sidecar there and did not here.\n\nKept as a divergence rather than deleted because it still is one: the other two schedule these on a timer and this one runs them in a loop, which is a different thing to operate and to reason about.

routines:stack-single:absent:qryx-trend.why: STILL ABSENT, and now for a stated reason rather than because nothing was scheduled at all. qryx-trend scans a SOURCE TREE; stack-up points it at its own checkout of the estate's repositories and there is none inside these containers. Mounting the operator's disk into a governance plane to look for crypto is a bigger decision than a missing routine, and it is not one to make on the way past.

routines:stack-single:absent:verdryx-dri.why: CLOSED on 2026-08-28 as `routine-verdryx-drift`, reading verdryx.db off the console's own volume read-only, the same store stack-k8s's quality-drift reaches. It SKIPS with a printed reason when ROUTINE_VERDRYX_BASELINE is unset, which is the honest default: a drift check needs a baseline somebody chose, and inventing one would compare against a number nobody stands behind. stack-up's routine skips for the same reason.

routines:stack-single:absent:idryx-detec.why: CLOSED on 2026-08-28. This deployment installed NO scheduler of any kind and now runs four routines behind `--profile routines`, as LOOPS rather than timers, because compose has no cron. That is the same shape the `record` profile already used. idryx-detect, as `routine-idryx-detect`, reading the shared bus read-only.\n\nKept as a divergence rather than deleted because it still is one: the other two schedule these on a timer and this one runs them in a loop, which is a different thing to operate and to reason about.

routines:stack-single:absent:mockryx-dri.why: STILL ABSENT. It needs the scenario files, which live in the mockryx repository and are not in this image, and it is opt-in in both other deployments anyway, which is why it matters least of the six.

routines:stack-single:absent:trailryx-se.why:
A DECISION since 2026-08-28, and no longer the gap this entry recorded on 2026-08-25. stack-single now seals the record; it just does not SCHEDULE it, which is what this family measures.

compose has no cron. So the `record` profile runs `record-seal` as a long-running service that seals on its own interval (`RECORD_SEAL_INTERVAL`, daily by default) rather than as a timer, and it is recorded in the services family as `services:stack-single:extra:record-seal`. The other two deployments schedule it: stack-up at 06:57 and stack-k8s at 05:27.

The four other `routines:stack-single:absent:*` entries stand and are still gaps: stack-single installs no scheduler of any kind, and this profile did not give it one.

min_severity.what: The HERALDYX_MIN_SEVERITY default: the floor below which the notifier stays quiet.

min_severity:stack-up:medium.why: stack-up is the local developer sandbox on one machine with one operator, where a medium-severity signal is worth reading and there is no mailbox to flood. The two real deployments sit at high. stack-k8s's manifest carries the same reasoning in a comment beside its own value. Read as a decision rather than a gap, but read by me from the code, not stated by anyone: if it is wrong, it is wrong here first.

ports.what: The fixed local port each component listens on. Two deployments putting the same component on different ports is what makes a runbook wrong.

ports:stack-k8s:unagreed:genaryx-console.why: Not a component port: `genaryx-console-lb` is a LoadBalancer Service in front of the console, so 443 is an ingress port and the console itself is still on the agreed 7420 in the same repo. It is deliberately EXCLUDED from stack-k8s's default kustomization because a cloud load balancer is metered, so a default install never creates it. stack-single reaches the same place with caddy. Recorded rather than filtered out in code, because 'Services of this type do not count' is a decision and decisions belong in this file where somebody can disagree with them.

services.what: Which components each deployment brings up.

services:stack-up:absent:console.why: stack-up serves a static dashboard out of python3 -m http.server instead of running the genaryx console. Deliberate: the console is a built web application and stack-up's whole argument is that it needs nothing but the binaries it installs into ~/.taipan/bin.

services:stack-up:extra:dashboard.why: The other half of services:stack-up:absent:console. The static dashboard on port 3000 exists only in stack-up.

services:stack-up:absent:policy-db.why: wardryx keeps its store on local disk under stack-up rather than in postgres. Deliberate: a sandbox that needs a database server is not a sandbox.

services:stack-single:extra:wg.why: stack-single is the one deployment meant to be reached from outside the box, so it ships a WireGuard endpoint. stack-k8s does the same job in a separate tunnel overlay outside manifests/, and stack-up is loopback-only by invariant.

services:stack-single:extra:caddy.why: TLS termination in front of the console, for the same reason as wg. In stack-k8s the equivalent is the LoadBalancer manifest, which is excluded from the default apply because it is metered.

services:stack-single:extra:init-volumes.why: A one-shot busybox container that creates the shared volume layout, not a running component. Kubernetes gets the same effect from PersistentVolumeClaims in 00-base.yaml and stack-up from mkdir in up.sh.

services:stack-up:extra:vouchryx.why: A DECISION, and his: the estate is one product installed by function («з можливістю встановлення за окремими функціоналами»), and `delegate` is one of those functions rather than part of the base stack. stack-up gained it first because it is the sandbox; stack-single and stack-k8s are step 3 of agent-market-research-2026-08/PLAN.md section 8 and will follow. Recorded as `extra` rather than by adding vouchryx to `agreed` on purpose: `agreed` is what every deployment brings up, and an opt-in profile is not that. Measured 2026-08-27 on a real ./up.sh --with-delegation: the gateway reports `delegation door: ON` and refuses a revoked token with HTTP 401, while the same launcher without the flag returns 200 to that same revoked token because the door never examines it. NOTE for whoever adds the other two: this file's model has no notion of a PROFILE, only of agreed/extra/absent, so a second and third deployment installing vouchryx will read here as two more `extra` entries rather than as one decision. That is a limit of C5 worth fixing when it bites, not a reason to write the wrong thing now.

services:stack-up:extra:costcrew.why: A DECISION, the `finops` profile from agent-market-research-2026-08/PLAN.md section 8 step 5, and the second of its kind after `delegate`. costcrew is an estate APP rather than a plane: a guest producer that writes the shared bus and calls nobody, and it enforces nothing. stack-up gained it first because it is the sandbox. Whether the two server deployments should carry it is his call and has not been asked. Measured 2026-08-28 on a real ./up.sh --with-finops: the console answers /healthz, puts 26 events on the bus, all 26 under the launcher's own trust domain rather than the console's default, and the seal in the same run recorded 9 of them. Under the console's default not one would have been recorded, which is why the profile sets -stack-host from the same variable the seal is given.

services:stack-single:extra:record-seal.why:
The `record` profile, step 3 of agent-market-research-2026-08/PLAN.md section 8, closing `@yurii 2026-08-25`'s decision that all three deployments seal the record. It replaces `routines:stack-single:absent:trailryx-seal`, removed the same day, which said stack-single did not mention trailryx anywhere. It now does.

Off by default, like `egress`: `WITH_RECORD=1 ./install.sh` builds the image and `docker compose --profile record up -d record-seal` starts it. One container running one serial loop rather than a timer, because compose has no cron and the record store takes no cross-process lock, so a second writer would be two minters of one shard. stack-k8s gets the same property from `concurrencyPolicy: Forbid`.

READ THIS ALONGSIDE the note on `services:stack-up:extra:vouchryx`: this file's model has no notion of a PROFILE, only agreed/extra/absent, so this is the second profile to land as an `extra` entry rather than as one decision spanning deployments. The limit is now costing two entries instead of one.

NOT a routine entry, deliberately. stack-single still installs no scheduler of any kind, so the four `routines:stack-single:absent:*` entries stand unchanged and true; this is a long-running service that seals on its own interval, which is a different shape from the cron the other two use.

services:stack-single:extra:focus-export.why: A ROUTINE that runs as a compose SERVICE, which is why it shows up in this family at all: the FinOps export, reading the gateway's own `traces` volume. compose has no cron, so the `routines` profile runs each as a long-lived loop, exactly as the `record` profile already ran trailryx-seal.\n\nSo the same work is a CronJob in stack-k8s, a timer entry in stack-up, and a service here. It is recorded in BOTH families on purpose: as a service because compose starts it, and in the routines family because that is the question somebody actually asks. This file's model has no notion of a routine that is also a service, which is the third time its shape has cost an extra entry, after the two profiles.

services:stack-single:extra:idryx-detect.why: A ROUTINE that runs as a compose SERVICE, which is why it shows up in this family at all: the identity sweep, reading the shared bus read-only. compose has no cron, so the `routines` profile runs each as a long-lived loop, exactly as the `record` profile already ran trailryx-seal.\n\nSo the same work is a CronJob in stack-k8s, a timer entry in stack-up, and a service here. It is recorded in BOTH families on purpose: as a service because compose starts it, and in the routines family because that is the question somebody actually asks. This file's model has no notion of a routine that is also a service, which is the third time its shape has cost an extra entry, after the two profiles.

services:stack-single:extra:verdryx-drif.why: A ROUTINE that runs as a compose SERVICE, which is why it shows up in this family at all: the quality drift check, reading verdryx.db off the console's volume read-only. compose has no cron, so the `routines` profile runs each as a long-lived loop, exactly as the `record` profile already ran trailryx-seal.\n\nSo the same work is a CronJob in stack-k8s, a timer entry in stack-up, and a service here. It is recorded in BOTH families on purpose: as a service because compose starts it, and in the routines family because that is the question somebody actually asks. This file's model has no notion of a routine that is also a service, which is the third time its shape has cost an extra entry, after the two profiles.

coverage.what: Both directions of the same question. Forwards: a component a repository's `runs` claims that no deployment installs. Backwards: a component a deployment installs that no repository claims. Subjects are DISCOVERED from estate.json's `runs` field and from what the deployments were read to install, never listed here. The second direction exists because `runs: []` is otherwise a way to leave this family with nothing to say: a repository that declares itself inert disappears from the check meant to find components nobody installs.

coverage:policy-db:claimed-by-no-reposit.why: A DECISION and not a gap: postgres, upstream. stack-single and stack-k8s run wardryx's store as a database server; no repository in this estate builds or owns it, so no `runs` can claim it. The check asks the coverage question in both directions, and upstream software installed beside our own is the honest exception to the second one. It is recorded rather than filtered out in code, because 'this one does not count' is a judgement and judgements belong in this file where somebody can disagree with them.

coverage:dashboard:claimed-by-no-reposit.why: A DECISION and not a gap: a static page stack-up serves with `python3 -m http.server`, and the other half of `services:stack-up:absent:console`. It is files in stack-up's own tree rather than a component any repository contributes. The check asks the coverage question in both directions, and upstream software installed beside our own is the honest exception to the second one. It is recorded rather than filtered out in code, because 'this one does not count' is a judgement and judgements belong in this file where somebody can disagree with them.

coverage:wg:claimed-by-no-repository.why: A DECISION and not a gap: WireGuard, upstream. stack-single is the one deployment meant to be reached from outside the box; see `services:stack-single:extra:wg`. The check asks the coverage question in both directions, and upstream software installed beside our own is the honest exception to the second one. It is recorded rather than filtered out in code, because 'this one does not count' is a judgement and judgements belong in this file where somebody can disagree with them.

coverage:caddy:claimed-by-no-repository.why: A DECISION and not a gap: Caddy, upstream. TLS termination in front of the console; see `services:stack-single:extra:caddy`. The check asks the coverage question in both directions, and upstream software installed beside our own is the honest exception to the second one. It is recorded rather than filtered out in code, because 'this one does not count' is a judgement and judgements belong in this file where somebody can disagree with them.

coverage:init-volumes:claimed-by-no-repo.why: A DECISION and not a gap: a one-shot busybox container that creates stack-single's shared volume layout. Not a running component and not anybody's product; see `services:stack-single:extra:init-volumes`. The check asks the coverage question in both directions, and upstream software installed beside our own is the honest exception to the second one. It is recorded rather than filtered out in code, because 'this one does not count' is a judgement and judgements belong in this file where somebody can disagree with them.
